Adaptively secure, splittable, and robust 
threshold unsigncryption
Yuxin Tong1,2, Shimin Li3, Zhiwei Wang1, Rui Zhang1* and Rui Xue1,2 
Abstract 
As a variant of the signcryption scheme, threshold unsigncryption operates among multiple receiver members 
through a (t, n) threshold process during the unsigncryption phase to improve security and robustness, and has been 
widely deployed in various applications such as cloud computing, blockchain, and electronic auctions. However, 
existing schemes only consider security under a limited static corruption model, where the adversary selects which 
parties to corrupt before the protocol begins. As a result, these schemes lack the flexibility to address more complex 
attack forms posed by real-world adversaries. To solve this issue, it is worth investigating threshold unsigncryption 
schemes with adaptive security. In this paper, we propose the first provably secure (t, n) threshold unsigncryption 
scheme in the standard model against adaptive corruption adversaries who can corrupt parties at any time dur-
ing protocol execution. The main contributions include: First, we provide the formal syntactic definition and security 
model of threshold unsigncryption schemes under the adaptive corruption model. Second, we employ the dual 
system technique to formally prove that the proposed scheme can achieve adaptive security in the standard model. 
Notably, our scheme is equipped with valuable properties such as non-interactivity, robustness, public verifiability, 
and splittable unsigncryption, significantly enhancing usability and functional completeness. Besides, we implement 
the proposed scheme on two types of elliptic curve groups with different security levels and evaluate its practical per-
formance under different thresholds. Experiments demonstrate that on a composite order group with 80-bit security, 
a single receiver only takes 16.61 s to perform the threshold unsigncryption phase when the number of receivers n 
is 20 and the threshold t reaches up to 18. As a pioneering adaptively secure threshold unsigncryption scheme, our 
work not only establishes a benchmark for future proposals but also broadens its application in scenarios requiring 
high-security levels and flexible key management, such as electronic voting.
Keywords  Threshold unsigncryption, Adaptive security, Splittable unsigncryption
Introduction
Encryption and digital signatures are fundamental 
cryptographic tools to safeguard information security 
in various communications. The signcryption scheme 
was initially proposed by Zheng (1997) in 1997. As a 
promising cryptographic primitive, signcryption can per-
form encryption and signature in a single logical step, 
providing confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and 
non-repudiation more efficiently compared to the tradi-
tional “Sign_then_Encrypt” approach. In general, confi-
dentiality prevents unauthorized parties from accessing 
plaintext, integrity ensures that data remains unaltered 
during transmission, authentication guarantees that the 
source of the message is genuine and trustworthy, and 
non-repudiation ensures that the signcrypters cannot 
deny the ciphertext they generated.
In recent years, numerous signcryption schemes have 
been proposed (Malone-Lee and Mao 2003; Chow et al.

As a result, they fall short of meeting the requirements

and enables at least t of them to collaborate to success-

Threshold unsigncryption (Koo et al. 2001) integrates 
the signcryption and threshold cryptography, distrib-
uting the unsigncryption task among a set of parties 
through a (t, n) threshold process. Figure 1 presents the 
workflow of threshold unsigncryption. The specific steps 
are as follows: (1) The sender A performs the key genera-
tion algorithm KeyGen to produce a public-private key 
pair (pkA, skA) . The trusted dealer runs the key genera-
tion algorithm KeyGen to generate the keys and distrib-
utes them to the receiver set B = {B1, ..., Bn} via a secure 
channel established through the Transport Layer Secu-
rity/Secure Sockets Layer (TLS/SSL) handshake protocol 
(Dierks and Rescorla 2008). At this point, each receiver 
Bi acquires the public key pkB , the private key share skBi , 
and the verification key vkBi . (2) The sender A invokes the 
signcryption algorithm Signcrypt on the plaintext M to 
produce the ciphertext C . (3) The sender A then trans-
mits C to the receiver set B . (4) The members of B collab-
orate to execute the threshold unsigncryption algorithm 
TUnsigncrypt . Receiver member Bi verifies the cipher-
text C and computes its unsigncryption share, which is 
then broadcast to the other receiver members through 
the secure channel established by the TLS/SSL proto-
col. When at least t parties {Bj}j∈R (where R ⊆{1, ..., n} 
and |R| ≥t ) provide valid unsigncryption shares, each 
receiver Bi can aggregate these shares to recover the 
plaintext M.
The primary design goal of threshold unsigncryption is 
to achieve the desired security requirements, including 
existential unforgeability under chosen-message attacks 
(UF-CMA) and plaintext indistinguishability under cho-
sen-ciphertext attacks (IND-CCA) in the n-party setting 
(where the adversary can corrupt at most t −1 members 
of the receiver set). Informally, UF-CMA means that 
unauthorized parties cannot generate valid ciphertexts. 
IND-CCA implies that any collusion involving fewer than 
t dishonest parties cannot steal any information about 
the plaintext.
Due to their advantages and security features, thresh-
old unsigncryption schemes are extensively utilized in 
contexts demanding high levels of security and flexible 
key management. These schemes are particularly valu-
able in electronic voting systems (Kohno et  al. 2004), 
distributed key management systems (Rafaeli and Hutch-
ison 2003), cloud computing (Armbrust 2009), block-
chain (Nakamoto 2008), and distributed databases (Özsu 
et al. 1999). Take electronic voting systems as an exam-
ple, voting information is signcrypted upon submission. 
Subsequently, the voting results can only be obtained 
when a sufficient number of authorized parties (such as 
election committee members) collectively engage in the 
unsigncryption process. This mechanism guarantees the 
security, integrity, and reliability of the voting process, 
thereby enhancing the credibility and fairness of the elec-
tronic voting system.

Existing threshold unsigncryption. Koo et al. (2001) 
proposed the first threshold unsigncryption in 2001 
by integrating the (t,  n) threshold technology based on 
Zheng’s signcryption scheme (Zheng 1997). Zhang et al. 
(2002) later introduced a similar scheme. However, these 
schemes lack formal security definitions and analysis, 
and are vulnerable to simple chosen ciphertext attacks. 
Subsequently, a series of identity-based threshold unsign-
cryption schemes (Li et al. 2005; Li et al. 2006; Yang et al. 
2007) were presented. However, they have proven unable 
to meet the UF-CMA or IND-CCA security require-
ments. To solve these problems, Herranz et al. (2010) and 
Selvi et al. (2010) presented secure threshold unsigncryp-
tion schemes in the traditional public key infrastructure 
(PKI) setting and the identity-based setting, respectively. 
However, their schemes were only proven to be secure in 
the random oracle model (ROM), which relies on heuris-
tic arguments and cannot be implemented in practice. 
Building on the threshold encryption scheme proposed 
by Boneh et al. (2006), Herranz et al. (2014) designed the 
first threshold unsigncryption scheme that is proven to 
be secure in the standard model. Table 1 provides a sum-
mary of existing threshold unsigncryption schemes.
In recent years, substantial research has focused on 
threshold encryption (Garg et  al. 2024; Boudgoust and 
Scholl 2023; Boneh et al. 2018) and threshold signature 
(Garg et al. 2024; Boneh and Komlo 2022; Yu and Wang 
2022). However, these efforts often fall short in provid-
ing both confidentiality and authentication, making them 
inadequate for application scenarios such as electronic 
auctions and electronic voting. Threshold signcryption 
(Yu and Wang 2023, 2021; Huixian et al. 2020) can effec-
tively achieve both confidentiality and authentication, 
but they focus on scenarios involving multiple senders 
and fail to achieve distributed management of decryption 
permissions. Although the works (Pang et al. 2016; Qiu 
et al. 2019; Yu et al. 2022) explore signcryption schemes 
involving multiple receivers, the authorized receivers still 
utilize their own keys for independent decryption, which 
also fails to effectively disperse the decryption permis-
sions. Consequently, the field of threshold unsigncryp-
tion that can simultaneously ensure confidentiality and 
authentication while enabling the distributed manage-
ment of decryption permissions requires ongoing atten-
tion and in-depth research.
Adaptive corruptions. We observe that existing prov-
ably secure threshold unsigncryption schemes only 
consider the limited static corruption model, where the 
adversary is required to determine which parties to cor-
rupt before the scheme initialization. Unfortunately, this 
model artificially limits the adversary’s abilities and can 
not accommodate complex and evolving attack forms. 
In contrast, the adaptive corruption model entitles the 
adversary to corrupt parties at any time based on its 
complete view. This model achieves superior security lev-
els and better caters to real-world scenarios Cramer et al. 
(1999), significantly outperforming the static corruption 
model in robustness. However, current research on adap-
tively secure threshold schemes primarily concentrates 
on threshold encryption Devevey et al. (2021); Libert and 
Yung (2013); Canetti et al. (1999) and threshold signature 
Bacho and Loss (2022); Bacho et al. (2023); Crites et al. 
(2023) schemes. These approaches fail to simultaneously 
address the dual requirements of confidentiality and 
authentication, thus limiting their applicability in scenar-
ios that demand both high security and the integration of 
encryption and authentication functionalities. Thus, it is 
worth investigating a provably secure threshold unsign-
cryption scheme under the adaptive corruption model.
However, it is difficult to transform a statically 
secure threshold unsigncryption scheme into an adap-
tively secure one. This is because the adaptive corrupt 
adversary prevents us from predicting its attack target 
in advance, which brings great challenges to the secu-
rity proof of the scheme. Herranz et  al. (2014) claim 
that their statically secure threshold unsigncryption 
scheme can be transformed into an adaptively secure 
one through techniques in Canetti et al. (1999); Jarecki 
et al. (2000); Lysyanskaya and Peikert (2001). However, 
the erasure technique adopted in Canetti et al. (1999) 
relies on parties to securely erase local data that is no 
longer used, which is difficult to ensure in practice. 
Although Jarecki et al. (2000); Lysyanskaya and Peikert 
(2001) avoid using the erasure technique, these works 
still necessitate substantial interaction among par-
ties, which requires synchronization among receiver 
members and high network bandwidth. Therefore, it is 
essential to construct non-interactive and lightweight 
adaptively secure threshold unsigncryption schemes.
Desired properties.  Under the premise of ensuring 
security, the threshold unsigncryption scheme promises 
to exploit valuable properties and further enhance its 
usability and functional completeness. Specifically, Non-
interactive implies that receiver members involved in the 
unsigncryption task can compute their partial unsign-
cryption results (called unsigncryption shares) with-
out interaction with each other. As mentioned in Shoup 
and Gennaro (2002), such non-interactive protocols are 
appealing as they eliminate the synchronization among 
receiver members and do not depend on network band-
width. Robustness means that even if a dishonest minor-
ity of parties within the receiver set deviates from the 
protocol, the uncorrupted parties can still successfully 
execute the unsigncryption process. Meanwhile, mali-
cious parties can be promptly identified and detected.

Another favorable property of threshold unsigncryp-
tion schemes is splittable unsigncryption. In this case, 
the threshold unsigncryption process can be divided into 
two phases: ciphertext verification and decryption. The 
ciphertext verification phase only requires public infor-
mation to verify the ciphertext validity and the signcryp-
tor identity. As a result, anyone can perform this phase, 
which is known as public verifiability. The decryption 
phase does not involve any information about the sender, 
thereby ensuring sender anonymity. This property is 
rewarding for applications (e.g., electronic auctions) 
that demand confidentiality and authentication, as well 
as anonymity and privacy at specific phases. In sum-
mary, the splittable unsigncryption exhibits the powerful 
ability to deliver a degree of anonymity on top of public 
verifiability.
To the best of our knowledge, there barely exists a 
provably secure threshold unsigncryption scheme that 
simultaneously integrates all the aforementioned desired 
properties. The scheme presented in Koo et  al. (2001) 
only has non-interactivity, while the schemes in Zhang 
et  al. (2002); Yang et  al. (2007); Selvi et  al. (2010) lack 
public verifiability and splittable unsigncryption capa-
bilities. Additionally, the schemes described in Li et  al. 
(2005); Li et  al. (2006); Herranz et  al. (2010) lack split-
table unsigncryption, although they have public verifi-
ability. As an exceptional case, the scheme proposed 
by Herranz et al. (2014) is equipped with all the above-
required properties. However, it only holds under the 
static corruption model. Therefore, exploiting these valu-
able properties while resisting strong adaptive corruption 
adversaries poses significant challenges and still deserves 
ongoing efforts.
In view of the deficiencies of existing threshold 
unsigncryption schemes, we initially raise the following 
question:
Is there an adaptively secure threshold unsigncryption 
scheme in the standard model that integrates all of the 
aforementioned desired properties?
Our contributions
Motivated by the deficiencies of existing work, we con-
duct in-depth research in the context of threshold 
unsigncryption and affirmatively answer the above ques-
tion. The main contributions are listed as follows:
•	 First, we provide the formal syntactic definition and 
security model of a (t,  n) threshold unsigncryption 
scheme under the adaptive corruption model. Given 
the absence of the security model against adaptive 
corruption adversaries for threshold unsigncryption, 
we thoroughly characterize the capability of an adap-
tive adversary that can corrupt at most t −1 parties 
in the n-party setting, theoretically defining the adap-
tive-CCA (chosen-ciphertext security under adaptive 
corruptions) and UF-CMA security.
•	 Second, we propose the first adaptively secure 
threshold unsigncryption scheme based on the dual 
system technique Waters (2009); Lewko and Waters 
(2010), and provide a formal security proof in the 
standard model. Notably, our scheme can exploit 
valuable properties such as non-interactivity, robust-
ness, public verifiability, and splittable unsigncryp-
tion, significantly enhancing its usability and func-
tional completeness. In addition, we compare the 
proposed scheme with existing threshold unsign-
cryption schemes (refer to Table  3), highlighting 
obvious superiority in terms of security and func-
tionality.
•	 Third, we evaluate the performance of the proposed 
scheme at both theoretical and implementation lev-
els. Initially, we conduct a theoretical analysis of the 
computational overhead and communication over-
head to demonstrate the feasibility and scalability of 
the scheme. Furthermore, we implement our scheme 
on two types of elliptic curve groups with different 
security levels and evaluate its practical performance 
under different thresholds (refer to Figs.  4,5, 6). 
Experiments show that on a composite order group 
with 80-bit security, a single receiver only takes 16.61 
seconds to perform the threshold unsigncryption 
phase when n is 20 and t reaches up to 18. As the first 
adaptively secure threshold unsigncryption scheme, 
our work can serve as a benchmark for future pro-
posals.
Overview of our techniques
One might intuitively think that simply concatenating 
a secure threshold encryption scheme with a standard 
signature scheme would construct a secure threshold 
unsigncryption scheme. However, the general con-
struction patterns of “ThresholdEncrypt_then_Sign” or 
“Sign_then_ThresholdEncrypt” fail to provide full security 
(i.e., IND-CCA and UF-CMA security under the static 
corruption model) (Herranz et  al. 2010; Herranz et  al. 
2014). The key reason is that the adversary can acquire 
the unsigncryption shares of receivers in the threshold 
unsigncryption. Informally, an adversary can replace 
certain information in the challenge ciphertext C⋆ cor-
responding to sender A⋆ by choosing a new fake sender 
identity ˆA⋆ to obtain a new (but invalid) ciphertext ˆC⋆ . 
Subsequently, the adversary utilizes ˆC⋆ to query the 
unsigncryption oracle and then exploits the broadcasted 
unsigncryption shares to recover the challenge plain-
text M⋆ , ultimately breaking the indistinguishability of

Our goal is further to design a fully secure threshold 
unsigncryption under the adaptive corruption model. 
It not only requires careful integration of the signature 
and encryption but also considers a powerful adversary 
who can corrupt parties at any time during the protocol 
execution, thus significantly increasing the complexity of 
scheme design and security proof. In addition to pursu-
ing adaptive security, it is advisable not to compromise 
on valuable properties, such as non-interactivity, public 
verifiability, and splittable unsigncryption.
Based on the above analysis, we ingeniously integrate 
identity-based encryption (IBE) and strongly unforgeable 
signature schemes to achieve our goal. More importantly, 
we employ the dual system technique Waters (2009); 
Lewko and Waters (2010) for the first time in threshold 
unsigncryption to realize non-interactive adaptive secu-
rity. The specific details are as follows:
We first thresholdize the Lewko-Waters IBE scheme 
(Lewko and Waters 2010) through secret sharing tech-
nology (Shamir 1979) to distribute the receiver’s private 
key among n parties. Following the similar methodol-
ogy as in Libert and Yung (2013), we then employ the 
dual system technique (Waters 2009; Lewko and Waters 
2010) to produce a CPA-secure threshold IBE scheme 
against adversaries adaptively choosing attack identities. 
For authenticating the sender’s identity, we integrate a 
strongly unforgeable signature scheme  to yield a sig-
nature σ on the output c of the threshold IBE scheme. 
However, this straightforward combination does not 
tightly couple the signature and encryption, thus failing 
to achieve the full security of threshold unsigncryption.
To implement a fully secure threshold unsigncryp-
tion scheme in the PKI setting, we introduce the 
Canetti-Halevi-Katz (CHK) paradigm (Canetti et  al. 
2004), which performs a strongly unforgeable one-
time signature ˜ on the ciphertext c and the signature 
σ . It not only tightly couples the signature and encryp-
tion but also provides CCA security in the PKI set-
ting, thereby achieving full security. To achieve the 
proposed scheme’s adaptive security, we apply the 
dual system technique to the threshold unsigncryp-
tion by constructing two types of semi-functional 
ciphertexts, as well as semi-functional unsigncryp-
tion shares and semi-functional private key shares. In 
addition, this modular design enables ciphertext veri-
fication and decryption operations to be performed 
independently, providing the opportunity to achieve 
the valuable properties of public verifiability and split-
table unsigncryption.

Strongly unforgeable signature
A signature scheme  = (.KeyGen, .Sign, .Verify) 
consists of the following three algorithms.
•	 (vk, sk) ←KeyGen(1) : The key generation algo-
rithm KeyGen takes the security parameter  ∈N as 
input and outputs the public verification key vk and 
the signature private key sk.
•	 σ ←Sign(sk, m) : The signature algorithm Sign takes 
the signature key sk and a message m as input and 
outputs a signature σ.
•	 0/1 ←Verify(vk, m, σ) : The verification algorithm 
Verify takes as input a verification key vk, a message 
m and a purported signature σ , and returns 1 if the 
signature is valid and 0 otherwise.
Definition 1  A signature scheme is strongly existen-
tially unforgeable under an adaptive chosen-message 
attack if no PPT adversary A making at most q signature 
queries has the non-negligible advantage in the following 
game.
Setup.	
The challenger runs (vk, sk) ←KeyGen(1) , 
gives vk to A and holds sk.
Query.	
The adversary A adaptively issues at most q 
signature queries. For i ∈{1, ..., q} , A sends mi 
of his choice to the challenger. Then, the chal-
lenger runs σi ←Sign(sk, mi) and sends σi to 
A.
Forgery.	
Finally, the adversary A outputs a pair 
(m, σ) . A wins if 1 ←Verify(vk, m, σ) and 
(m, σ)  = (mi, σi) for all i ∈{1, ..., q} . A ’s advan-
tage is defined as Adv(A) = Pr[A wins].
A strongly unforgeable signature scheme against adver-
saries who can make at most q = 1 signature query in the 
above game is called a secure one-time signature scheme.
Adaptively secure threshold unsigncryption
We delve into the threshold unsigncryption scheme 
between a single sender A and a series of receivers 
{B1, · · · , Bn} . Specifically, the sender A executes the sign-
cryption phase to generate ciphertext, ensuring the con-
fidentiality of the message and verifying its origin from 
A. The receiver’s private key is distributed among vari-
ous parties {B1, · · · , Bn} through secret sharing technol-
ogy, effectively avoiding single points of failure or abuse 
issues. As a result, the set of receivers reaching the

In this section, we propose a (t,  n) threshold unsign-

standard model against adaptive corruption adversar-

Security services analysis
In this section, we further demonstrate that the proposed 
adaptively secure threshold unsigncryption scheme effec-
tively provides security services such as confidential-
ity, integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. The 
detailed analysis is as follows.
On the one hand, we rigorously prove that the pro-
posed scheme achieves adaptive-CCA security, which 
indicates that even if t −1 receivers are corrupted by a 
powerful adaptive adversary, the adversary is still una-
ble to obtain any information about the plaintext. As a 
result, this scheme naturally ensures the confidentiality 
of the plaintext. Furthermore, the robust adaptive-CCA 
security ensures the scheme’s resilience against complex 
chosen-ciphertext attacks under adaptive corruptions, 
offering protection against a range of weaker adversarial 
scenarios, such as static corruption, selective corruption, 
semi-honest adversaries, and passive adversaries. As a 
result, the scheme can effectively withstand various real-
world attacks, including eavesdropping, chosen-plaintext 
attacks, key recovery attacks, and even chosen-ciphertext 
attacks under static corruption (Static-CCA).
On the other hand, our proposed scheme is proved 
to be UF-CMA secure, which means that unauthorized 
parties are unable to generate valid ciphertexts. In other 
words, valid ciphertexts can only be produced by author-
ized parties with private keys. Thus, UF-CMA security 
simultaneously guarantees integrity, authentication, and 
non-repudiation. Moreover, a UF-CMA secure thresh-
old unsigncryption scheme is capable of resisting various 
real-world attacks, including tampering attacks, data for-
gery attacks, identity forgery attacks, reputation attacks, 
and so on.
In addition, we compare the security services pro-
vided by the proposed threshold unsigncryption scheme 
with those of existing schemes. As shown in Table  2, 
our scheme not only ensures confidentiality, integrity, 
authentication, and non-repudiation but also offers adap-
tive-CCA security under the adaptive corruption model, 
thus providing a higher level of security.

Discussion and future work
We innovatively propose an adaptively secure threshold 
unsigncryption scheme. Compared with directly inte-
grating the general method of achieving adaptive security 
(Canetti et al. 1999; Jarecki et al. 2000; Lysyanskaya and 
Peikert 2001) into the statically secure threshold unsign-
cryption scheme, our method uses the well-known dual 
system technique (Waters 2009; Lewko and Waters 2010). 
This approach avoids extensive interactions between 
parties and significantly reduces the cost of achiev-
ing adaptive security. Although our approach exhibits a 
slight performance trade-off relative to current statically 
secure threshold unsigncryption schemes (Herranz et al. 
2010; Selvi et  al. 2010; Herranz et  al. 2014), it success-
fully enhances the security level to adaptive security. As 
indicated in Tables 4 and 5, the utilization of a composite 
order bilinear group (which is marginally slower than a 
prime order group) leads to slightly increased commu-
nication and computational overhead in the proposed 
scheme compared to Herranz et  al. (2010); Selvi et  al. 
(2010); Herranz et al. (2014).
Building on the above discussion, future research will 
aim to enhance the performance of adaptively secure 
threshold unsigncryption schemes to achieve an optimal 
balance between security and efficiency. In particular, it 
is worth investigating more efficient, provably secure,

Conclusion
In this paper, we present the first adaptively secure 
threshold unsigncryption scheme, in which multiple 
receiver members jointly perform the unsigncryption 
phase through a (t, n) threshold process. Using the dual 
system technique and composite order groups, we prove 
under the standard model that our scheme achieves 
Adaptive-CCA and UF-CMA security in a n-party set-
ting against adaptive corruption adversaries. Meanwhile, 
our scheme integrates valuable properties including non-
interactivity, robustness, public verifiability, and splittable 
unsigncryption. Furthermore, we implement and evalu-
ate the performance of the proposed scheme by deploy-
ing two types of elliptic curve groups. Experiments show 
that a single receiver only takes 16.61  s to perform the 
unsigncryption phase when n is 20 and t reaches up to 18 
on the elliptic curve group with 80-bit security. In future 
work, we aim to explore adaptively secure threshold 
unsigncryption schemes without composite order groups 
or bilinear mappings to improve efficiency, thereby ena-
bling broader applications in scenarios that demand high 
security and flexible key management, such as electronic 
voting and electronic auctions.

Abstract: As a variant of the signcryption scheme, threshold unsigncryption operates among multiple receiver members through a (t, n) threshold process during the unsigncryption phase to improve security and robustness, and has been widely deployed in various applications such as cloud computing, blockchain, and electronic auctions. However, existing schemes only consider security under a limited static corruption model, where the adversary selects which parties to corrupt before the protocol begins. As a result, these schemes lack the flexibility to address more complex attack forms posed by real-world adversaries. To solve this issue, it is worth investigating threshold unsigncryption schemes with adaptive security. In this paper, we propose the first provably secure (t, n) threshold unsigncryption scheme in the standard model against adaptive corruption adversaries who can corrupt parties at any time dur- ing protocol execution. The main contributions include: First, we provide the formal syntactic definition and security model of threshold unsigncryption schemes under the adaptive corruption model. Second, we employ the dual system technique to formally prove that the proposed scheme can achieve adaptive security in the standard model. Notably, our scheme is equipped with valuable properties such as non-interactivity, robustness, public verifiability, and splittable unsigncryption, significantly enhancing usability and functional completeness. Besides, we implement the proposed scheme on two types of elliptic curve groups with different security levels and evaluate its practical per- formance under different thresholds. Experiments demonstrate that on a composite order group with 80-bit security, a single receiver only takes 16.61 s to perform the threshold unsigncryption phase when the number of receivers n is 20 and the threshold t reaches up to 18. As a pioneering adaptively secure threshold unsigncryption scheme, our work not only establishes a benchmark for future proposals but also broadens its application in scenarios requiring high-security levels and flexible key management, such as electronic voting.
